answers.text: Biodiversity is the huge variety of living things on Earth. Every organism has a job: tiny algae in the sea give out most of our oxygen, fungi and bacteria break down dead leaves and make the soil fertile, bees and birds and bats pollinate flowers, and plants use sunlight to make food for almost everyone. People need it for food, medicines and homes, and farmers kept many crop varieties so that one failure would not ruin the harvest.

Between 1950 and 2000 dictatorships actually grew slightly faster than democracies, about 4.42 percent against 3.95. Growth depends on many things like population, the global situation and cooperation from other countries. Among poor countries the gap is tiny, 4.34 against 4.28. So democracy does not guarantee development, but we can expect it not to be behind dictatorships.

Shoot tips also have dividing cells, so plants have growth zones at the tips called apical meristems that make them grow longer.

Light atoms like carbon and oxygen have equal protons and neutrons, but heavy atoms like iron and uranium have many more neutrons than protons. All the protons carry a positive charge and repel each other. Neutrons are neutral, so they reduce this repulsion by keeping the protons apart and by strengthening the nuclear force, which holds the nucleus together.

When you choose one option you give up the others, and the value of what you give up is the opportunity cost. A farmer with limited land, water and labour can grow barley or wheat, and the production possibility curve slopes downward showing the trade-off: to grow more barley some wheat must be sacrificed, which is the opportunity cost. Points on the curve show the maximum output with no wastage, and this helps firms and governments plan.

Jowar, bajra and ragi are the main millets in India. They are called coarse grains but are very nutritious, and ragi has a lot of iron, calcium and roughage. Jowar is the third most important food crop by area and production and grows in moist areas on rain with hardly any irrigation. Bajra grows on sandy and shallow black soils and ragi on dry regions with red, black and sandy soils.

People used to think all the power of a government must sit with one person or group in one place. With democracy this changed: people are the source of all political power and rule themselves through self-government institutions, so power should be spread among as many citizens as possible. Modern democracies share power among organs of government, levels of government, social groups, and parties and pressure groups.

In 2025 Punjab had severe floods because of heavy monsoon rain on the Satluj, Beas and Ravi. Natural causes were very heavy rain made worse by western disturbances, rain in Himachal and Jammu and Kashmir, and rivers already high. Human causes were weak old embankments, houses and farms built too near the rivers, silt that reduced capacity of rivers and dams, and late or unclear warnings. It caused loss of life, relief camps, damaged crops, dairy farms, roads and bridges and health problems.

India is the biggest producer and consumer of pulses in the world. Pulses like tur, urad, moong, masur, peas and gram are the main source of protein in a vegetarian diet. They need little moisture and survive in dry conditions. Since they are leguminous they fix nitrogen from the air, so all except arhar restore soil fertility and are grown in rotation with other crops.

Electricity is used in so many ways that its per capita consumption is an index of development. It is generated in two main ways: fast flowing water drives hydro turbines, giving hydro electricity, and burning coal, petroleum and natural gas drives turbines for thermal power. Hydro uses a renewable resource, with projects like Bhakra Nangal and Damodar Valley, while thermal stations use non-renewable fossil fuels, but the electricity produced is exactly the same.

In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh a militant guerrilla movement started in the early 1920s which the Congress could not approve. The government had closed forests so people could not graze cattle or collect fuelwood, and forced them to do begar for roads, so they revolted. Alluri Sitaram Raju led them: he praised Gandhi and urged khadi and giving up drink, yet said India could be freed only by force. The rebels attacked police stations; Raju was captured and executed in 1924 and became a folk hero.

Women took part in large numbers in the Civil Disobedience Movement. During the salt march thousands came out to hear Gandhi, joined protest marches, made salt, picketed shops selling foreign cloth and liquor, and many went to jail. They were from high-caste urban families and rich peasant households and saw service to the nation as a sacred duty. But their public role did not change how women were seen: Gandhi thought women should look after home and family, and the Congress was reluctant to give them positions of authority.
